stories.label: Strait of Hormuz ship traffic drops to single vessel
stories.summary: One commodity vessel transited Hormuz on Monday — the lowest daily count since May 7 — and hours after Washington unveiled its 'economic D-Day' package another ship was struck in the strait. Lead with the number one: a waterway that normally carries about a fifth of seaborne oil has been emptied not by a blockade but by underwriters and shipowners deciding the transit is uninsurable, which is how a chokepoint closes without anyone announcing a closure. The mechanism to teach is that transit volume is the real sanctions scoreboard: war-risk premium, charterer refusal and AIS transponder blackouts do the work an actual mine barrage would, at no cost to Tehran. Who is affected first: Gulf and Asian importers and every economy downstream of that crude, not the US Treasury that set the pressure campaign in motion. Follow the earlier Bessent sanctions and rial pieces rather than repeating them — this is the physical consequence of both. Carry the Iranian source (Mehr, relaying Reuters shipping data) and the US one (The War Zone) side by side and flag which claims each stands behind; attribute the strike itself carefully, since neither the vessel's damage nor the attacker has been independently confirmed.

stories.label: Venezuela earthquake death toll exceeds 6,500
stories.summary: The death toll from Venezuela's earthquake has passed 6,500, with 226,696 people recorded as having received medical assistance — figures given by National Assembly Speaker Jorge Rodríguez on Telegram. Lead with the two numbers together: the ratio of injured to dead is what tells the reader whether hospitals are still functioning, and 226,696 treated against 6,509 killed describes a health system absorbing a mass-casualty event across weeks, not hours. The mechanism to explain is why the toll keeps climbing after the shaking stops — crush injuries, water and sanitation failure, and the slow work of clearing collapsed masonry, which is where the sanctioned-economy constraint on heavy equipment and imported medical supplies becomes lethal. Who is affected: Venezuelans, overwhelmingly poor and in unreinforced housing; who holds power: a government that is also the only source of the count. Attribute every figure to Rodríguez and to TASS's relay of it, and say plainly that no independent verification is available in this feed and that the death toll has been revised upward repeatedly. Latin America has been absent from our coverage — this is the region's story, not a footnote to US policy.

stories.label: The Mecca Pact: What Do We Actually Know?
stories.summary: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey have signed a joint defence agreement and almost nothing about its text is public. Write the absence as the story: lead with what is actually known — the signatories, the date, the venue — and then with the specific questions the agreement's secrecy leaves open, above all whether it contains a mutual-defence clause and whether Pakistan's nuclear deterrent is implicitly extended to Riyadh. The mechanism to teach is that a defence pact's value lies entirely in its automaticity: an alliance that obliges consultation is a communiqué, one that obliges response is a security guarantee, and only the text distinguishes them. Structural why for our reader: three of the largest Muslim-majority militaries aligning outside the US security architecture is the most consequential development in the ummah's strategic geography in years, and it is happening while Washington cancels exercises in Asia and fights Iran. Who is not consulted: the parliaments of all three states. Be rigorous about the difference between what has been confirmed, what officials have implied, and what analysts are inferring — the Diplomat's own framing is that the details are scarce, so do not fill the gap with speculation.

stories.label: US Supreme Court hands a win to Trump over mail-in ballot restrictions
stories.summary: The Supreme Court lifted part of the block on Trump's executive order restricting mail-in ballots, months before midterms in which control of Congress is close — but a separate injunction still blocks a key part of the plan, so the order is only partly in force. Lead with that split, because the precise state of the law is what most coverage will blur. The mechanism to explain is who sets election rules: the Constitution assigns the time, place and manner of federal elections to the states and to Congress, so an executive order reaching into ballot procedure is a claim of presidential authority over an area the presidency has never held — and the Court's willingness to let it operate while litigation continues is itself the ruling that matters. Who is affected: voters who rely on mail ballots — disabled, elderly, rural and overseas — a group that does not map neatly onto either party but does map onto whoever finds it hardest to reach a polling place. Note this is a shadow-docket-style interim posture, not a merits judgment, and say what remains enjoined.

stories.label: Two cops booked for 'torturing man to death' in Bahawalpur
stories.summary: Kahror Pacca police registered a murder case against two of their own constables, Muhammad Khan and Aurangzeb, over a man tortured to death in custody; the complaint came from Pitras Masih, a municipal employee, whose name signals a Christian complainant pressing a case against police in southern Punjab. Lead with the names on both sides — the accused and the complainant — because custodial death reporting usually erases both. The mechanism to explain is why an FIR against constables is the exception rather than the rule: the same station that holds the body controls the initial evidence, the post-mortem and the first information report, so a case exists only when someone outside the police is willing to complain and survive doing so. Structural why: torture is not a lapse in Pakistani policing but its default investigative method for people without money or connections, and prosecutions almost never reach conviction — give the reader what happens next procedurally, and what usually happens instead. Name the dead man if Dawn does; count him as a person, not as a case number.

stories.label: Will China Rewrite the Rules of Global Supply Chains?
stories.summary: Beijing is writing its own corporate due-diligence and supply-chain responsibility standards and exporting them to the countries its firms operate in. Lead with what a standard actually does: it decides which audits count, which certifiers are accredited, and therefore which suppliers can sell — so whoever writes the standard controls market access without a tariff or a treaty. The mechanism to teach is standard-setting as soft infrastructure, the same lever the EU pulls with its own compliance stack and that this week's Tesla door-handle recall showed China already pulling on product safety. Who is affected: manufacturers across Africa, South and Southeast Asia now facing two incompatible compliance regimes and the cost of satisfying both; who holds power: the ministries and industry bodies drafting text no exporter votes on. Structural why for a strategic reader — the contest over supply chains is being fought in rulebooks, not ports, and a country that adopts Chinese standards is harder to decouple than one that merely trades with China. Attribute the analysis to the Diplomat's author and be concrete about which Chinese standards exist today versus which are proposed.

stories.label: Centre plans to privatise 11 airports in five bundles
stories.summary: India will privatise 11 airports as five bundles, deliberately pairing a profitable airport with a loss-making one — Amritsar with Kangra-Gaggal, Varanasi and Gaya with smaller fields — so the bidder cross-subsidises the small airport from the large one's earnings. Lead with the bundling itself, because that is the whole design: the state is selling the obligation to serve unprofitable places along with the right to earn from profitable ones, which is how public-service loss is transferred to a private balance sheet without a subsidy line in the budget. The mechanism to explain is where airport money actually comes from — landing fees are the small part, and retail, parking, real estate and fuel throughput are the rest, so the winning bidder's return depends on passenger spending at Varanasi, not on flights to Kangra. Who is affected: passengers at the small airports, whose service level now depends on a concession contract's terms rather than a ministry's mandate, and airport workers moving to private employment. Structural why: bundling is a fiscal technique spreading across South Asian infrastructure — get the concession length and the tariff-setting rules into the piece, since those decide whether it works.

stories.label: Europe's heatwaves threaten insurers' earnings, rating agency S&P says
stories.summary: S&P says European heatwaves are now a threat to insurers' earnings through claims linked to heat-related deaths and illness, especially among older people — and that premiums will rise in response. Lead with the reframing that lands hardest: heat has crossed from a weather story into a life-and-health underwriting story, which means the financial system has begun pricing climate mortality directly rather than through flood and windstorm damage. The mechanism to explain is how an insurer responds to a repriced risk — it raises premiums, tightens terms, or withdraws from the segment, and all three transfer the cost to the people most exposed, who for heat are the old, the ill and those without cooling. Who holds power: three rating agencies whose assessments move capital before any regulator acts; who is affected: pensioners in southern Europe first, and then everyone in the risk pool. Structural why for a global reader — the same actuarial logic applied to the Gulf, South Asia and the Sahel, where wet-bulb exposure is far worse, would price insurance out of reach entirely, which is why climate adaptation is becoming a question of who can still buy cover. Attribute the earnings claim to S&P and give the report's own numbers.

stories.label: Rakbank Islamic enables access to Bitcoin trading through its Islamic banking platform
stories.summary: A licensed Islamic bank in the UAE is now offering Bitcoin trading inside its shariah-compliant platform — the first time most of its customers will be able to buy crypto without leaving the Islamic banking perimeter. Lead with the fiqh question the product implicitly answers, because that is what our reader will want and what business coverage omits: scholars have divided for a decade over whether Bitcoin is māl (property with recognised value) and whether its volatility constitutes gharar, and a bank launching the service means a shariah board has issued a ruling. Get that ruling and its reasoning, or say clearly that the bank has not published it. The mechanism to explain is what a bank actually adds: custody, KYC and a regulated counterparty, which converts a bearer asset into a claim on an institution — the same inversion as Hong Kong's bank-distributed stablecoin, so cross-reference rather than repeat. Structural why: Gulf regulators are absorbing crypto into the licensed banking system rather than banning or ignoring it, and Islamic finance is where the doctrinal argument for doing so has to be made. Single source; do not overstate retail availability or imply an endorsement the bank has not given.

stories.label: US sanctions Iranian cyber actors as UK discloses power plant attack
stories.summary: Washington sanctioned several Iranian nationals over attacks on critical infrastructure days after Britain disclosed an intrusion at a small power plant. Lead with the word 'small': the plants that get compromised are not the flagship stations with security operations centres but the minor generators and water utilities whose control systems are old, internet-exposed and maintained by two people. The mechanism to explain is why sanctioning named individuals is a weak instrument here — an OFAC designation freezes assets in a jurisdiction the target never enters and bars transactions they never make, so its real function is attribution and signalling, not denial of capability. Who is affected: the operators of thousands of unglamorous utilities across Europe and the Gulf that are inside the blast radius of a state-level conflict they have no part in; who holds power: the governments escalating that conflict while leaving the exposed infrastructure unfunded. Structural why: the Iran war has a cyber front where the targets are chosen for softness rather than value, and the response so far is a press release. Attribute the UK intrusion to the reporting rather than to a confirmed government finding, and be precise about what the sanctions allege versus what has been proven.

stories.label: Dozens of ex-lawmakers, staff landed at military firms since 2015
stories.summary: A Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists report names 31 former members of Congress and senior staff who left the armed services committees for the weapons industry since 2015 — and the new destination is Silicon Valley, not Boeing: Palantir hired two ex-HASC members, Anduril's chief strategy officer ran the Senate committee's Republican staff, and a former HASC staff director now sits on a naval commission while lobbying for a maker of the unmanned vessels it will recommend. Lead with that last case, because it is the whole mechanism in one person: the same individual advises on the requirement and sells the product. The structural why for a technically literate reader is that defence-tech startups cannot win through the Pentagon's multi-year acquisition process, so they buy the people who know how to route around it — which is why an autonomous-weapons firm is valued at $61 billion. Include the STOCK Act detail — seven armed services members in violation this year — as evidence of how weak the existing guardrail is. Ground every claim in the named report and public disclosures, and attribute Responsible Statecraft's framing as its own; the underlying facts are documented, the inference about causation is the outlet's.

stories.label: NHS England to offer women 'gamechanging' free home testing kits for cervical cancer
stories.summary: England will post free self-sampling HPV kits to women who have missed cervical screening — up to four million are not up to date, and only about two-thirds attend. Lead with the four million, because the number is the argument: the barrier to eliminating cervical cancer is not the test's accuracy but attendance, and a clinic appointment requiring time off, transport and a physical examination is a filter that removes exactly the women at highest risk. The mechanism to explain is what changed technically — screening now looks for high-risk HPV DNA rather than for abnormal cells under a microscope, and an HPV assay works on a self-collected vaginal swab, which cytology could not; the science is what makes the logistics possible, not the other way round. Who is affected: women who have been counted as non-compliant when they were in fact unreachable. Structural why for a global reader: cervical cancer kills overwhelmingly in low- and middle-income countries with no screening programme at all, and self-sampling is the one modality that does not require a clinician per patient — which is why the WHO elimination target depends on it far more outside Britain than inside. Keep the 2040 elimination target attributed to the NHS.

stories.label: ESA to Adapt Ariane 6 for Nuclear-Powered Argonaut Missions
stories.summary: ESA will modify Ariane 6 to launch Argonaut lunar landers carrying a Radioisotope Power System — not for the first mission, but for later ones. Lead with the physical reason: the lunar night lasts about fourteen Earth days, and no solar array or battery mass a lander can carry survives it, so anything meant to operate for years at the Moon needs heat and power from decay, not sunlight. The mechanism to explain is what 'adapting the rocket' actually means — launching a radioisotope source obliges the vehicle to be qualified against the case where it fails, so the changes are about containment and range safety rather than performance, and that is why the requirement lands on the launcher and not the payload. Structural why for our reader: Europe has depended on American plutonium-238 and has been developing americium-241 as its own supply precisely to avoid that dependency, so this is a sovereignty story wearing a spacecraft-engineering costume — the same logic as chip fabrication, applied to an isotope only a few states can make. Say clearly what is committed and what is planned; ESA has not flown this yet.

stories.label: Maternal obesity programs offspring metabolic dysfunction via small extracellular vesicle-mediated epigenetic remodeling
stories.summary: A Nature Communications paper reports a physical carrier for something long observed but unexplained: children of obese mothers inherit metabolic dysfunction, and the study identifies small extracellular vesicles as the vehicle that remodels the offspring's epigenome. Lead with the courier, not the correlation — the finding is a mechanism, and mechanisms are what turn an association into something that could be interrupted. Explain plainly what an sEV is: a membrane-wrapped parcel of regulatory RNA that one tissue releases and another absorbs, which is how a mother's metabolic state can write instructions into a fetus without changing a single gene sequence. Structural why for our reader: this is intergenerational risk with a biological address, and it matters most where obesity and diabetes are rising fastest — the Gulf, Egypt, Malaysia, Pakistan — which are also the places least likely to be represented in the trial data that follows. Be exact about the limits: this is mouse and cell work with human relevance argued, not demonstrated, and say so rather than letting the headline claim stand alone. Open access — link the paper so readers can check it.

stories.label: Trump removes Syria from 'terrorism list'
stories.summary: Washington formally struck Syria from the State Sponsor of Terrorism list and delisted Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham — the group that led the government now being armed. Lead with what the delisting unlocks mechanically: SST designation is the statutory hook for export controls, arms-transfer bans and the sanctions architecture layered on top of it, so removal converts Syria from an embargoed state into an eligible recipient of US military aid in a single Federal Register act. The structural why: a designation that survived 47 years of Syrian governments was lifted by executive determination, not legislation, which is the same rulemaking-over-lawmaking pattern seen in this week's H-1B fee. Note who is not in the story — Syrians displaced by both the old government and the new one, and the Caesar Act penalties that Congress, not Rubio, controls.

stories.label: Ambush in South Sudan kills peacekeeping troops
stories.summary: Two UNMISS peacekeepers were killed when armed men ambushed a patrol heading to Pajut in Jonglei state. Lead with the route, not the casualty count: UNMISS patrols are the only outside presence in much of Jonglei, and attacking one closes the corridor through which civilian protection and food convoys move. The mechanism to explain is that a peacekeeping mandate depends on freedom of movement it cannot enforce — when patrols stop, the protection-of-civilians sites become the whole of the mission. Structural why: South Sudan is drifting back toward the 2013-style split between the president's and the first vice-president's camps, and the people who pay first are the Jonglei civilians who lose the patrol, not the troop-contributing countries who lose the soldiers. Name the peacekeepers' nationalities if the sources give them.

stories.label: Airstrikes on Civilians in Rakhine Will Increase, Say Myanmar Military Defectors
stories.summary: Defectors from Myanmar's air force say the bombing of Rakhine villages is not collateral — it is the stated method for holding the last townships the military still controls after losing the ground war to the Arakan Army. Lead with the defectors' own account of how targets are chosen, because that is the evidentiary core: insiders describing intent is what turns 'airstrike killed civilians' into a documented policy. The mechanism: an army that cannot hold territory with infantry substitutes aircraft, and aircraft cannot discriminate at the resolution village-level control requires. Structural why: Rakhine is where the Rohingya were driven out in 2017 and where those who remain are now under the bombs of the same air arm, with the state's collapse in the region removing even the pretence of accountability. Note it is a single specialist source; attribute the defectors' claims explicitly.

stories.label: Family, legal team of Imaan and Hadi voice concerns over medical facilities at Adiala jail
stories.summary: Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chatta — both human rights lawyers — were sentenced by an Islamabad sessions court in January and their families now say Adiala jail cannot provide basic medical care. Lead with the named people and the specific denial, not the abstraction: prison medical neglect is how a sentence becomes an open-ended punishment no court reviewed. The mechanism to explain is that jail medical provision sits outside the appellate record, so the conditions of detention are unreviewable even while the conviction is under appeal. Structural why: Pakistan's pattern of prosecuting the lawyers who represent the detained converts legal defence itself into a punishable act — connect to the wider clampdown the joint opposition met about the same day.

stories.label: Opinion | Trump Unleashes Scott Bessent on Iran
stories.summary: Bessent announced the Treasury will target every Iranian revenue stream worldwide, not just oil — the phrase used in Washington was 'economic D-Day'. Lead with the scope change: previous rounds sanctioned buyers of Iranian crude, this one targets the intermediaries, shippers, banks and shell structures that move any Iranian money anywhere, which is a secondary-sanctions posture aimed at third countries. The mechanism to explain is that a revenue-wide campaign works through foreign banks' compliance departments, not through US enforcement, so the binding effect lands on Chinese refiners, Gulf trade houses and Turkish and Pakistani intermediaries who must choose between Iranian business and dollar access. Follow the earlier rial and Hormuz pieces: Tehran's economy minister says a counter-plan was drawn up in advance, and Mokhber's reply frames it as the 47th year of the same policy — carry both Iranian responses so the story is not told only from Washington.

stories.label: Ford to speak in Hamilton following Canada-U.S. trade deal fallout
stories.summary: Ontario's premier answered new US tariffs by threatening to cut electricity exports and critical minerals — 'you won't get a grain of sand.' Lead with the asymmetry that makes the threat credible: Ontario supplies power directly into the New York, Michigan and Minnesota grids, and a subnational government controls that valve without needing Ottawa. The mechanism to explain is that trade retaliation has migrated below the national level, where a province can impose costs on specific US states faster than any federal countermeasure clears. Structural why: this is what happens when tariff policy is set by executive discretion — the response also stops being diplomatic and becomes infrastructural. Note the sentiment spread across sources (0.31): Indian outlets lead on the threat, Canadian ones on the domestic fallout.

stories.label: ECC approves bonded storage of imported petroleum products
stories.summary: Pakistan's Economic Coordination Committee will let foreign fuel suppliers build bonded storage on Pakistani soil at their own expense, for re-export as well as domestic supply — a direct structural answer to the Hormuz closure. Lead with who pays and who owns: the state gets strategic depth without spending, the supplier gets duty-deferred inventory inside a consuming market, and the fuel in the tanks is not Pakistan's until it clears customs. The mechanism to explain is the bonded-warehouse rule itself — goods sit in-country untaxed and unowned, which is why this is cheaper than a state reserve and also weaker than one in a crisis. Follow the Hormuz shutdown pieces: this is the first concrete inland consequence, and it makes Pakistan a re-export node for a region it used to be a terminus of.

stories.label: Documents Reveal Trail of Unreported Millions From Israeli Military to U.S. Universities
stories.summary: Documents show research money flowing from Israel's Ministry of Defense and its arms manufacturers into US universities without appearing in the federal database built to track foreign gifts. Lead with the reporting gap itself, with the dollar figure and the named institutions: Section 117 of the Higher Education Act requires disclosure of foreign funding above a threshold, and what the documents show is the threshold being routed around. The mechanism to explain is how the money is structured — grants routed through foundations, subawards and industry partners are not classified as foreign government gifts, so the legal duty never triggers. Structural why: a database designed to make foreign influence on American research legible is only as good as the categories it recognises, and defence ministries are the parties best resourced to find the seam. This is a single investigative source — attribute the documents and say what could not be confirmed.

stories.label: Energy-hungry AI data centers spur new power transformer technology
stories.summary: Data-centre demand has made the transformer — a device essentially unchanged since the 1880s — the binding constraint on grid expansion, and the money is now going into solid-state replacements. Lead with the physical fact readers will not have: a conventional transformer is copper, steel and oil, takes years to order, and cannot switch or route power; a solid-state one is a semiconductor stack that can, which turns a passive component into a controllable node. The mechanism to explain is why that matters beyond AI — SSTs let a grid accept variable renewable input and DC loads without the fixed-ratio conversion step, so the constraint AI created may be what finally funds it. Structural why: infrastructure gets modernised when a rich buyer needs it urgently, and everyone else inherits the result — worth naming who is not in that queue, since grid-transformer lead times are already rationing electrification across South Asia and Africa.

stories.label: Wildlife trafficking spreads across social media, putting thousands of species at risk
stories.summary: Six weeks of monitoring in mid-2025 found primates, birds, snakes, frogs and orchids advertised for sale across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. Lead with the breadth — thousands of species, four platforms, one short observation window — because the surprise is that this is open commerce, not a dark-web trade. The mechanism to explain is that recommendation systems built to match niche interest to niche supply are exactly what a trafficker needs, and platform enforcement is keyword-based against a trade that renames its goods weekly. Structural why: the enforcement burden falls on source countries in the tropics that have neither jurisdiction over the platforms nor visibility into the listings, while the demand and the advertising revenue sit elsewhere. Give the study's own numbers and name the platforms.

stories.label: Watch - Inside Cape Town's data hub deal
stories.summary: A Cape Town golf course became a R3-billion logistics hub and is now set to host two of the city's largest data centres — via a R100 land swap, a reclassification of the data centre as a 'warehouse', and an environmental assessment deferred to a later stage. Lead with the R100 and the word 'warehouse': the price is the accountability story and the classification is the mechanism. Explain how it works — planning approval attaches to a land-use category, so calling a power-hungry, water-cooled facility a warehouse routes it past the water and electricity scrutiny a data centre would attract, in a city with a recent day-zero drought. Structural why: African data-centre buildout is being negotiated one municipal reclassification at a time, and the public learns the terms after the land has moved. Name the officials and the companies the reporting names.

stories.label: Ads and tracking infiltrated TVs. Now they're coming for monitors.
stories.summary: The computer monitor was the last display you could buy without an ad business inside it; LG and others are now shipping monitors with the same webOS content platform, tracking and bundled software that made smart TVs surveillance devices. Lead with the loss of the escape hatch — the standard privacy advice was 'use a monitor', and that advice is expiring. The mechanism to explain is automatic content recognition and the economics behind it: the panel is sold near cost because the recurring revenue is the viewing data, so a display that never phones home is now the premium product. Structural why: hardware margins collapsing into data margins is the same move that took over TVs, phones and cars, and it arrives without a purchase decision the buyer can see. Tell readers concretely what to check before buying and what to disable.

stories.label: How Europe is killing makers and micro-entrepreneurs
stories.summary: A European electronics marketplace operator lays out what the EU's product-compliance stack — GPSR, the responsible-person requirement, WEEE and battery registration, and per-country packaging schemes — costs a seller shipping a few hundred boards a year. Lead with the fixed cost per country, because that number is the whole argument: compliance that is rounding error for a large importer is a hard floor that a one-person hardware business cannot clear. The mechanism to explain is regulatory fixed cost as a barrier to entry — rules written to police anonymous mass imports apply identically to a named individual selling 200 units, and the compliance burden does not scale down. Structural why: this is how a market consolidates without anyone intending it, and it matters beyond Europe because the EU's product rules are copied into other jurisdictions. 942 points on Hacker News — the readership feeling it is the site's own. Attribute the cost figures to the author and note the vendor's interest.

stories.label: Government Proposes New Six-Figure Fee for H1-B Visas
stories.summary: DHS proposes a $103,265 fee on most new H-1B applications — including people already inside the US changing status, which is the detail that turns a hiring tax into a deportation risk for workers mid-career. Lead with the number and who pays it: Indian and Pakistani engineers make up the large majority of H-1B holders, and Dawn is covering it as a Pakistani story, not an American one. The mechanism to explain is that the fee is set by rulemaking, not by Congress, so it takes effect without a vote. Structural why: the US is converting a skilled-migration channel into a revenue and rationing instrument, pricing out startups and mid-size employers while leaving the largest tech firms able to absorb it.

stories.label: U.S. military says it struck drug boat in eastern Pacific killing 2
stories.summary: US Southern Command killed two people on a boat in the eastern Pacific and named no victims, filed no charges, and produced no evidence beyond the phrase 'operating along established narcotrafficking routes'. Lead with the asymmetry: two dead, zero due process, first such strike in months — the resumption is the news. The mechanism to explain is legal, not military: designating traffickers as narcoterrorists converts a law-enforcement interdiction, which requires arrest and trial, into a lethal targeting decision made inside a combatant command. Note who is absent from the story — the dead are presumed Latin American and remain unnamed, and no coastal state has been said to consent.

stories.label: Asim Munir visits Tehran as Pakistan revives Iran peace mediation
stories.summary: Pakistan's army chief, not its foreign minister, is carrying a message to Tehran that Indian reporting says originated with Trump — and he arrived on the day Washington prepared its 'economic D-Day' sanctions package. Lead with the channel, not the trip: Islamabad's mediation runs through the military, with the interior minister attached and the civilian foreign ministry largely absent. Structural why: Pakistan is monetising its position between Washington and Tehran at the moment its own credit is being repriced, and a mediation track that lives in GHQ rather than the foreign office survives changes of government but answers to no parliament. Follow-up context: this is the second leg of a clustering tour after the ISI chief's Bahrain visit, and it lands against Iran's currency record low and the Hormuz transit-fee threat.

stories.label: Four labourers killed by unknown assailants in Balochistan's Pishin district
stories.summary: Four road workers were shot dead by armed men on the Quetta-Chaman highway in Pishin — the victims are labourers on a state infrastructure project, which is precisely why they were reachable. Lead with what they were doing when they were killed: building the road that connects Quetta to the Afghan border. The mechanism to explain is that Balochistan's insurgency now targets the construction workforce rather than the security escort, because unarmed migrant labour from Punjab and Sindh is the softest point in a hard corridor, and each killing raises the security premium on the next contract. Name the victims where Dawn does; count them as workers, not as an incident number.

stories.label: Gary, Indiana still without power; U.S. to unveil "economic D-day" sanctions against Iran; Israel bombs mosque, desalination plant in Gaza
stories.summary: Israel struck a mosque and a desalination plant in Gaza on the same day. Write the desalination plant as the lead, not the footnote: Gaza's aquifer is over 95% unfit to drink, so desalination is not infrastructure among others — it is the water supply, and destroying it converts a strike into a months-long thirst for everyone downstream of that pipe. The mechanism to explain is that water plants are protected objects indispensable to civilian survival under Additional Protocol I, which is why their destruction is legally distinct from hitting a barracks. Pair it with the mosque strike as the same pattern: the things a besieged population cannot replace. Ignore the Gary and sanctions items in this digest — they are separate stories.

stories.label: Houthis say they attacked vessel off Saudi Arabia
stories.summary: A Houthi ballistic missile hit the Amzan, a Saudi-owned VLCC capable of carrying two million barrels, in the Red Sea off Yanbu — and the target is the point. Lead with the shift: the Houthis have spent two years hitting Israel-linked and Western shipping; a Bahri supertanker is Saudi state-adjacent tonnage on a Saudi export route, which reopens a front Riyadh believed it had bought out of. The mechanism to explain is insurance, not ordnance: war-risk premiums on Red Sea transits are priced off the last incident, so one hit near Yanbu reprices every cargo leaving the terminal and pushes marginal volumes back around the Cape. Structural why: Yemen's war has become a lever on Gulf export economics that costs the Houthis one missile to pull.

stories.label: Nvidia senior manager linked to Supermicro scheme smuggling AI servers to China
stories.summary: Taiwan has indicted nine people — reportedly including an Nvidia senior manager and two Supermicro staff — for forging export paperwork to move restricted AI servers into China. Lead with the seniority: this is not a broker in Shenzhen, it is people inside the companies whose compliance departments are the enforcement mechanism. The mechanism to explain is that US export controls on AI accelerators are enforced through documents, not customs inspection — the end-user certificate is the control — so a forged destination field defeats the entire regime at near-zero cost. Structural why: Taiwan, not Washington, brought the charges, which shows where the chokepoint physically sits and how much of US chip policy depends on another state's prosecutors.

stories.label: Saudi construction hiring slows sharply as giga-project ambitions are scaled back
stories.summary: Saudi construction hiring is falling as the giga-projects are trimmed — and the people who absorb that first are migrant labourers from Pakistan, Bangladesh, India, Nepal and the Horn of Africa, whose legal residency is tied to the employer that no longer needs them. Lead with the labour side, which the business coverage of Vision 2030 usually omits. The mechanism to explain is kafala arithmetic: a scaled-back project does not produce unemployment in Saudi Arabia, it produces repatriation and unpaid final wages, and the remittance shortfall lands in the sending country's current account within a quarter. Structural why: NEOM-scale capex was financed against oil at a price that has not held, so the retrenchment is a fiscal signal, not a project-management one.

stories.label: How a Network of Volunteers Is Liberating Critical Court Records for Everyone
stories.summary: A volunteer network, Habeas Dockets, is publishing US immigration court records that are technically public but have never been available online — you had to physically walk into a courthouse to read them. Lead with that gap: the records were never sealed, they were just unindexed, and unindexed is functionally secret at national scale. The mechanism to explain is that habeas petitions are where detention without charge becomes visible; scraping and publishing them turns thousands of individually invisible cases into a dataset that shows patterns — which judges, which facilities, how long. Structural why: the reader should see that the modern accountability battle is not over classification but over retrieval cost, and that a handful of volunteers with scrapers can change what a state is able to do quietly.

stories.label: Hackers infecting Android car systems to build proxy botnet
stories.summary: Malware is infecting Android-based in-car infotainment units and enrolling them as residential proxy nodes. Lead with why a car is the ideal victim: it is an always-on Android device with a mobile data plan, no antivirus, no user who ever checks it, and an update cycle measured in years — the perfect host for traffic laundering. The mechanism to explain is the proxy botnet business model: the attacker does not want your car, it wants your IP address, which is then rented to whoever needs traffic that looks like an ordinary consumer. Structural why: car makers ship a general-purpose computer and then support it like a radio, and there is no recall process for a vehicle that has been quietly turned into infrastructure for someone else's fraud.

stories.label: Tesla to recall almost three million vehicles over hidden door handles
stories.summary: Chinese regulators are forcing Tesla to recall nearly three million vehicles over flush electronic door handles — the concern is that after a crash cuts power, occupants and rescuers cannot open the doors. Lead with the number and the failure mode: a design chosen for drag coefficient and brand identity becomes a trap in exactly the situation doors exist for. The mechanism to explain is regulatory, not mechanical: China is writing a national standard on door handles that binds every EV maker including Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely, and Tesla is simply the largest installed base caught by it. Structural why: the world's biggest EV market now sets the safety floor that Western regulators will inherit, reversing who exports standards to whom.

stories.label: A New Framework for How the Brain Compresses Our Noisy World
stories.summary: Neuroscientists are replacing the filing-cabinet model of categorisation — the brain sorts things into boxes — with a compression model: categories are whatever lets the nervous system predict the next input with the fewest bits. Lead with the reframing, not the experiment. The mechanism to explain is that under this view a category is a lossy code, so the information the brain discards is chosen by what it expects to need, which is why perception is systematically biased rather than merely noisy. Structural why for a technically literate reader: this is the same objective that trains a machine-learning model, and the convergence is the interesting claim — but the piece should be precise about what is demonstrated versus what is analogy.

stories.label: Corners in focus: Metasurface enables motion tracking without digital image processing
stories.summary: A City University of Hong Kong team built a metasurface that performs corner detection optically — the edge-finding step normally done in software happens in the light itself, using an azimuthal Hilbert transform, before any sensor reads it. Lead with what is removed: no processor, no frame buffer, no power budget for the operation. The mechanism to explain is that corners are the features tracking algorithms actually key on, so moving that one operation into the optics collapses the front end of a vision pipeline into a passive component. Structural why: the compute cost of machine vision is the reason cameras that watch continuously need mains power and cloud backhaul; optical preprocessing is one of the few routes around it, and this one comes out of Hong Kong rather than a US lab.

stories.label: 'Barrel bomb mufti' Ahmad Hassoun handed life sentence in Syria trial
stories.summary: Damascus's Fourth Criminal Court sentenced Assad's grand mufti to life for 'inciting civil war and sectarian strife' — the first time the old regime's clerical apparatus, not its generals, has been convicted. Lead with what the charge is and is not: incitement, not the barrel bombs he blessed, which is the gap between the nickname and the indictment. Who is affected: the families of the killed, who get a verdict that names words rather than weapons; who holds power: a transitional judiciary trying regime figures in ordinary criminal courts rather than a special tribunal, which sets the precedent for every case that follows. Teach the mechanism — domestic prosecution is faster and cheaper than international justice but binds only Syria and carries no extradition weight over those who fled. The three sources diverge sharply in tone (divergence 0.33): Al Jazeera frames it around the death penalty he faced, DW around a cleric's fall. Report the disagreement. Note the sentence is life, not death — say who asked for what.

stories.label: Iran's currency hits new record low as US prepares to announce more sanctions
stories.summary: The rial opened at 2.02 million to the dollar — a record — with Washington promising sanctions stronger than those already in place, six months after the February 28 US-Israeli strikes. Lead with the number and what it buys: the exchange rate is a price index for imported medicine, wheat and machine parts, so a currency record is a household cost story before it is a markets story. Who is affected: salaried Iranians and importers paid in rial, not the state, which prices oil in dollars; who holds power: the correspondent banks that decline transfers, which is why humanitarian exemptions exist on paper and fail in practice — the same mechanism as this week's seized-cargo-for-EB-patients piece, so cross-reference rather than repeat it. Explain the structural why for a strategic reader: sanctions now work through expectations, not enforcement — the announcement moves the rate before any measure takes effect. Two sources, US and Indian, and they diverge (0.35): Yahoo relays a market print, The Hindu frames it as pressure. No Iranian or Gulf outlet in today's feed carried the rate — attribute the level to the market report and give the date-stamp.

stories.label: Burnham Hails Ukraine's Defiance as Similar to Defeat of Nazis
stories.summary: Allies convened in Kyiv on Independence Day and pledged to bolster air defences before winter; the British prime minister reached for a Second World War analogy. Do not write the rhetoric — write the magazine depth behind it. The pledge that matters is interceptors, and the same day's TASS report (attribute it as Russian state media, and treat the claim as contested) says European arsenals are too depleted to supply them, which is why the frozen-Russian-assets argument is being reopened in Brussels. Lead with the gap between a guarantee and a stockpile: air defence is consumable, one missile per incoming drone, and European production lines run at a fraction of expenditure. Who is affected: Ukrainian civilians in a fourth winter of strikes on the grid; who holds power: a handful of European missile makers whose annual output caps what any summit can promise. Three sources — Bloomberg, SCMP and Al Jazeera — report the same day very differently; Zelensky's line that Ukraine 'wants peace but won't simply surrender' is the substance, the Nazi comparison is not.

stories.label: U.S. Cancels Marines Drills With South Korea
stories.summary: Washington scrapped the Twin Dragons amphibious exercise with South Korea, scheduled for next month — the latest American pullback in Asia since the war in Iran. Lead with the causal chain readers in Seoul, Manila and Taipei are already drawing: a Middle East war is consuming the amphibious shipping and Marine rotations that underwrite deterrence in the Pacific, so a cancelled drill is an accounting statement about force availability, not a diplomatic gesture. Who is affected: allies whose defence planning assumes a US amphibious force that is now elsewhere; who holds power: a single Pentagon scheduling decision that no treaty partner votes on. The mechanism to teach is that exercises are the visible part of readiness — units that do not rehearse a landing lose the capability within a training cycle, so the signal is real even when the rhetoric is unchanged. Note honestly what is not known: whether this is deferral or drawdown, and what Seoul has been told. Single US source; attribute the pullback framing to the WSJ's reporting.

stories.label: Living on the Edge of South Sudan's Toxic Floodplains
stories.summary: Five years after the 2021 floods drowned Unity State, 70 percent of it is still underwater — and the water sits on top of dozens of submerged oil wells, so the marsh people were displaced into is the same marsh their produced water leaches through. Lead with the permanence: this is not a flood that receded, it is a new hydrology, and the health effects are already legible in maternity wards. Who is affected: millions displaced within their own state, drinking and washing in it because there is nowhere upslope; who holds power: the consortium operators and the government ministry that shares their revenue and also regulates them — name both, and say who has published contamination data and who has not. The structural why for the reader: oilfield water management is a cost line, and in a state with no functioning environmental enforcement it is simply never paid. Single-source original reportage; keep the medical claims attributed to the clinicians quoted, and give the reader the one number that anchors it — how much of Unity State is still submerged.

stories.label: Moody's lifts Pakistan sovereign rating to B3 from Caa1
stories.summary: Moody's raised Pakistan two notches to B3, stable, a month after S&P's upgrade, citing better governance and easing external vulnerability. Lead with what a rating actually is: a price, not a verdict — B3 is still deep speculative grade, and the concrete consequence is the coupon Islamabad pays when it next returns to the eurobond market. Who is affected: not investors first but the budget, where every basis point of external borrowing cost competes with subsidy and development spending; who holds power: three private firms whose opinions are hardwired into other institutions' investment mandates, which is why a ratings note moves more money than a finance ministry's own accounts. Give the reader the structural why — Pakistan's improvement is largely reserves and rollovers secured through the IMF programme and bilateral deposits, meaning the upgrade certifies successful refinancing rather than new earning capacity. Pair it honestly with the FBR penalty story in today's Pakistani press: the same fiscal squeeze that pleases Moody's is being felt as a 25-fold late-filing penalty on taxpayers. Single Pakistani source; treat the rating action as fact and the causal claims as Moody's own.

stories.label: Standard Chartered (STAN) becomes first bank to distribute Hong Kong dollar stablecoin
stories.summary: A licensed bank, not a crypto exchange, is now the distribution channel for one of Hong Kong's two regulated stablecoins — Anchorpoint's, in institutional rollout since August 12, with HSBC preparing its own for the second half of the year. Lead with the inversion: for a decade stablecoins were a way around banks, and the regulated version arrives through them. Who is affected: exporters and remitters across Asia who settle in Hong Kong dollars and can now move them on-chain without leaving the banking perimeter; who holds power: the HKMA, whose licence decides who may issue, which converts an open-network instrument into a permissioned one. The mechanism worth teaching: a bank-distributed stablecoin is a claim on a bank's reserve management, so the risk moves from smart-contract failure to balance-sheet failure — a different question, not a smaller one. The structural why: Hong Kong is building a dollar-pegged settlement rail under Chinese sovereignty, which is the actual geopolitical content. Single source; keep the two named licensees straight and do not imply retail availability.

stories.label: KPMG Australia's troubles deepen as it cuts 5% of its workforce
stories.summary: KPMG Australia is cutting about 5 percent of its people — 27 partners and 360 employees — disclosed inside its own annual earnings release, amid a whistleblower-led scandal and a consulting slowdown. Lead with the two numbers together: partners are owners, and a firm that sheds 27 of them is repricing its ownership, not trimming staff. Who is affected: the employees, and the public bodies whose audits and advisory work the Big Four hold; who holds power: a partnership that audits the companies it also sells consulting to, which is the conflict the whole Australian Big Four cycle since the PwC tax-leaks affair has failed to resolve. The mechanism for the reader: consulting revenue subsidises audit pricing, so when advisory demand falls the audit function is squeezed — the accountability service gets cheaper exactly when the firm is under scrutiny. Structural why: an unlisted partnership discloses what it chooses to, so a whistleblower is the only reporting line that reaches the public. Single US source; attribute the scandal characterisation, give the headcount as disclosed, and cover the Australia dateline the audit flagged as an Oceania gap.

stories.label: Xiaomi Develops Its Own AI Mobile Chip in Challenge to Qualcomm
stories.summary: Xiaomi launched the Xring O3 system-on-chip for its flagship phones, displacing Qualcomm and MediaTek in the part that matters most. Lead with what designing a phone SoC actually costs — a decade of failed attempts and a nine-figure annual budget is the entry fee, which is why only Apple, Huawei, Samsung and now Xiaomi have paid it. Who is affected: Qualcomm and MediaTek, whose Chinese volume is the base of their business, and every Chinese handset maker now under pressure to follow; who holds power: TSMC, because the design is Xiaomi's and the fabrication is not — an in-house chip is sovereignty over the blueprint, not over the factory, and that distinction is the whole China semiconductor question in one product. The reader is technically literate: give them the node, the on-device AI claim, and what 'more power-efficient' is measured against. Structural why: export controls made dependence on a US supplier a strategic risk, so vertical integration is now a hedge rather than a margin play. Single source; treat Xiaomi's performance claims as vendor claims.

stories.label: The UAE is fighting AI hackers with AI of its own
stories.summary: Attacks on Emirati banks, aviation and energy systems have climbed since the war with Iran began, and the state's answer is a domestic AI security industry rather than imported vendors. Lead with the asymmetry that makes this a real story: AI collapses the cost of the attacker's slowest step — reconnaissance and tailored phishing at scale — while the defender's cost stays roughly fixed, so automating defence is not an upgrade but a requirement to stay level. Who is affected: customers of Gulf banks and users of an aviation hub the region's trade routes run through; who holds power: a state building sovereign security capability partly to avoid depending on US and Israeli vendors for the software that watches its own critical infrastructure. The structural why for the reader: cyber capability is becoming an import-substitution industry in the Gulf, the same logic as domestic refining or desalination. Single-source original reporting from a specialist outlet; attribute attack-volume figures to whoever counted them, and be precise that 'AI defence' here means detection and triage, not autonomous response.

stories.label: Everything I own, owned
stories.summary: A first-person account of a total personal compromise — every device and account — that reached 1,038 points and 287 comments on Hacker News in a day, which is the public-attention signal worth acting on. Read the post before writing and lead with the pivot: the single credential or device that turned one breach into all of them, because that chain is the transferable lesson and the reason developers recognised themselves in it. Who is affected: anyone whose recovery paths all terminate in one email account or one phone number, which is nearly everyone; who holds power: the platforms whose account-recovery design decides whether a compromise is contained or total, and who face no liability when it is not. The mechanism to teach is concentration of trust — SSO, password managers and phone-based recovery each reduce friction by making one secret load-bearing. Structural why: consumer security advice optimises for password strength while the actual failure mode is recovery-flow design. Single self-published source: verify each claim is the author's own account, attribute it as such, and do not name any accused party the post does not evidence.

stories.label: Poisoned waters: Indigenous communities fight to protect Thailand's Kok River
stories.summary: Indigenous communities in northern Thailand are organising to defend the Kok River, whose contamination arrives from upstream and across a border they cannot petition. Lead with the geography, because it is the mechanism: a river carries the externality downstream, so the people bearing the heavy-metal load have no jurisdiction over its source, and no Thai regulator can inspect a mine outside Thailand. Who is affected: farming and fishing communities whose land tenure, drinking water and cultural claim to the river are the same claim; who holds power: the upstream operators and the two governments that have not built a joint monitoring regime. Teach the reader what transboundary water law actually offers — data-sharing and consultation, almost never enforcement — and what testing has and has not been published. Structural why: Southeast Asia's mineral supply chains are being pushed into weakly governed upstream basins precisely because the downstream cost is someone else's. Single specialist source and thin on measurements; give concentrations only where a named test supports them, and address the Southeast Asia and Global South science gaps the audit flagged.

stories.label: Long-term landscape risk dynamics and human-environment interactions in the Qiantang River Basin (1980-2020)
stories.summary: Forty years of land-cover data for the Qiantang River Basin — the watershed that drains through Hangzhou into the bay with the world's largest tidal bore — measured as ecological risk rather than as growth. Lead with the finding, not the method: say which decade the risk curve turned and what land conversion drove it, because the interest for a strategic reader is that China's most-studied urbanisation is now long enough to have a before and after. Who is affected: tens of millions living in a basin whose flood behaviour is set by upstream cover; who holds power: provincial planners who allocate construction land, and whose decisions this dataset makes auditable after the fact. The mechanism to explain simply: landscape risk indices convert fragmentation and patch loss into a single number, which is useful for trends and misleading as an absolute — say so plainly. Structural why: the same 1980-2020 arc is now beginning in South and Southeast Asian deltas with far less monitoring, so the value is as a template. Accepted-manuscript preprint stage — flag that it is peer-reviewed but not the final version of record, and avoid the jargon entirely in the lead.

stories.label: Nvidia As The New Banker For AI Gold Rush
stories.summary: Nvidia now finances the customers who buy its chips — equity stakes, backstopped leases and vendor credit to the neoclouds and model labs whose purchase orders become its revenue. Lead with the circularity, not the earnings preview: when the seller funds the buyer, demand and financing are the same number counted twice, which is the mechanism behind every capex boom that ended badly (Lucent and the CLECs in 2000 is the exact precedent). Who is affected: not Nvidia shareholders first, but the pension and index money that owns the largest position in the world through funds nobody chose deliberately, and the sovereign AI programmes in the Gulf and India buying at the top of the cycle. Who holds power: one supplier that sets both the price of compute and the credit terms on which it is bought. Give the reader the arithmetic — what share of the revenue Wall Street is waiting on is financed by Nvidia itself. Note the three sources diverge sharply in tone (sentiment divergence 0.37): Investing.com relays Citi's buy-side optimism, Hindustan Times frames it as Wall Street dependency. Report the disagreement rather than averaging it.

stories.label: Why Vijay shelved the Parandur project despite Chennai's need for another airport
stories.summary: Tamil Nadu's new chief minister cancelled the Parandur greenfield airport in the Assembly, four years after farmers in thirteen villages began a continuous protest against the land acquisition it required. Lead with what actually moved the project: not a feasibility study but an unbroken village sit-in that outlasted a government. Who is affected on both sides — roughly a thousand families whose paddy land and the Eekkadu lake system were inside the footprint, and a Chennai airport already past its design capacity with no second field. Who holds power: a state that can acquire land under a 2013 law whose consent and social-impact clauses states have systematically diluted. The structural why for the reader: greenfield infrastructure in dense agrarian India has no empty land to use, so every project is a transfer from cultivators to travellers, and the only question is whether the transfer is negotiated or imposed. Say plainly what is unresolved — a replacement site is promised but unnamed, which means the same fight relocates rather than ends. Both sources are Indian; keep the electoral framing thin, the durable fact is the acquisition precedent.

stories.label: BTC, ETH price news: Bitcoin pauses near $77,000 ahead of Warsh's Jackson Hole debut
stories.summary: Write the Fed story, not the crypto story: Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole address as chair is the event every asset class in this report is positioned around — Asian equities down, Brent and Treasury yields lower, bitcoin flat after a 21 percent week. Lead with the asymmetry that matters to a reader outside the US: one unelected official's framing of the policy path reprices the dollar, and therefore reprices the import bill, the debt service and the currency of every country that borrows in it — Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria, Indonesia. The mechanism to explain is why a Fed chair's tone moves more capital than most governments' budgets: dollar rates are the world's discount rate, and Jackson Hole is where the committee's read on them is signalled before it is voted. Warsh's own record is the substance — a persistent inflation hawk who dissented toward tighter policy after 2008 — so give the reader what a hawkish debut would cost emerging-market borrowers in concrete terms. Treat the 21 percent weekly crypto move as evidence of liquidity expectations, not as the subject. Single US source; attribute the market levels to CoinDesk and keep them as of the Asian session.

stories.label: Casualties reported in Israeli attacks on Khan Younis
stories.summary: A man died on Monday morning at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis of wounds from an Israeli strike the day before; the Israeli military says it struck a Hamas commander and has not said whether he was hit. Continuation of injustice is the development — write the interval, not the incident: the gap between a strike and a death is the collapsed medical system, and Nasser is the last functioning referral hospital in southern Gaza, operating on generator power with rationed blood and no ICU capacity. Who is affected: a named man in a named hospital, and every casualty who becomes a delayed death because there is no surgical theatre free. Who holds power: the party choosing the strike, and the party controlling what crosses into Gaza to treat its results. The mechanism worth teaching the reader is that 'targeted' is a claim about intent, not about outcome, and that an unverified target claim published alongside a confirmed death is not a balance of facts — report the death as established and the targeting as asserted. Sourcing note for honesty: Iranian state media relaying Gaza medical sources is the only account in today's feed; no wire, and no Palestinian outlet, carried it. Attribute the medical source explicitly and give the count as reported.

stories.label: New Zealand to introduce bill banning social media for children under 16
stories.summary: Luxon's government will introduce a bill barring under-16s from social media, and the prime minister conceded in the same breath that it 'won't be simple' — that admission is the lead, because the entire policy reduces to a question he has not answered: how a platform establishes a user's age without checking every adult's identity too. Lead with the mechanism, because it is the whole consequence: age assurance means either government ID upload, facial age estimation, or data-broker inference, and all three convert an anonymous account into a verified one for the whole population, not just for children. Who holds power: three or four foreign platforms that will build one compliance system and apply it globally, which is why Australia's 2024 ban matters far beyond Australia — it wrote the template New Zealand is now copying, and the template travels to jurisdictions with no privacy regulator at all. Who is affected: teenagers cut off from the networks where diaspora and minority communities organise, and every adult who will now prove their age to speak. Give the reader the harms Luxon names — addictive design, sleep, mental health — and note honestly what the evidence base for a hard age cutoff does and does not show. Two sources, Philippine and Indian; neither is a New Zealand outlet, so lean on Luxon's quoted words rather than local political framing.

stories.label: Iran seizes, sells US oil cargo for EB patients
stories.summary: Iran's judiciary says a US oil cargo seized in the Persian Gulf in 2023 was sold under court order and the proceeds directed to patients with epidermolysis bullosa — the rare genetic condition whose sufferers, known in Iran as 'butterfly children', cannot get the imported Mepilex dressings that are their only treatment because sanctions cut the payment channel, not the export licence. Lead with that loop, because it is the entire story: a state monetises a confiscated tanker cargo to buy medicine it is nominally permitted to import but practically cannot pay for. Who is affected: a few hundred children whose skin blisters at contact and who need the dressings weekly; who holds power: the banks that decline the transfer rather than any sanctions regulator, which is the mechanism readers most often miss — humanitarian exemptions exist on paper and fail at the correspondent bank. Report the seizure honestly as an act Washington calls piracy and Tehran calls enforcement of a court judgment, and note that a one-off cargo sale funds a patient group for months, not a health system. Sourced solely to Iranian state media relaying the judiciary; attribute throughout and treat the proceeds figure as claimed. Complements this week's sanctions-and-Hormuz arc from the medical side rather than the oil-price side.

stories.label: Gunmen kill two security operatives, seize rifles in Plateau
stories.summary: Gunmen attacked Tanjol and Tarai in Jol District of Riyom LGA, killed two security operatives and took their rifles. Lead with the rifles, not the deaths: every successful raid on a checkpoint transfers weapons from the state to the attackers, so the local security force is the armoury, and each attack makes the next one cheaper. That arithmetic is why Plateau's violence compounds rather than burns out. Who is affected: farming villages on the Jos Plateau where the same communities have been raided for a decade along a fault line the shorthand calls farmer-herder but which is really about land tenure — indigene-versus-settler rules that make citizenship in Plateau State hereditary and lock migrants out of land title permanently. Who holds power: Abuja, which owns every armed officer, since Nigerian states have no police of their own — the same constitutional gap that left Niger State issuing statements after the Borgu mosque abduction two days ago. Do not write this as the third instalment of that story; write the weapons-capture mechanism that neither earlier piece covered. Single Nigerian source, casualty count as reported, no group named — say so.

stories.label: Ethereum lending app Term Finance loses $8.5 million after attacker buys voting power
stories.summary: Nobody broke Term Finance's code — the attacker bought enough governance tokens to vote themselves the permissions that drained $8.5 million from a vault, then the protocol closed the product and revoked the governance layer that made it possible. Lead with that distinction, because it is the lesson: this was not an exploit of a bug but an exercise of a documented feature at a price the market set. The mechanism to teach is governance capture as a purchasable attack — if control of a contract is a liquid token, then the cost of taking over the contract is a quote on an exchange, and any treasury smaller than the token's float is underwriting its own theft. Who is affected: depositors in a custom vault, and Yearn, which had to state publicly that its standard vaults were untouched because Term's bespoke governance wrapper, not Yearn's code, was the hole. Who holds power: whoever can afford the float. The structural why for the reader: 'decentralised governance' and 'security' are in direct tension — the more freely voting power trades, the cheaper an administrative takeover becomes, and this is the same class of failure as Beanstalk in 2022, which should have settled the question. Single US source; the loss figure is estimated and Term's own account.

stories.label: 31 ex-lawmakers, staffers joined military firms in past 10 years
stories.summary: A Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists count finds 31 former members of Congress and senior armed-services staff moved into weapons firms in a decade — 21 lawmakers who sat on the committees writing the NDAA, plus 10 committee staff directors. Lead with the named case that shows the mechanism working in real time: Chris Vieson, ex-staff director of House Armed Services, now sits on the congressional commission advising on the Navy's future while registered as a lobbyist for Saronic, which builds the unmanned vessels that commission is chartered to promote. The structural why, and the reason this is a tech story: the new arrivals are not Lockheed and Boeing but Anduril, Palantir and Andreessen Horowitz, and the pitch that carries them past the Pentagon's acquisition rules is speed — software cycles beat procurement cycles, so the process built to stop exactly this is waived on the grounds that it is too slow. Who is affected: taxpayers in a budget the report's author says only ever rises, and every country on the receiving end of autonomous systems procured without the review a fighter jet would get. Include the disclosure failures by name (seven armed-services members in STOCK Act violation this year) and the author's own conclusion that disclosure law without prosecution changes nothing. Sourcing discipline: the underlying report is public and its subjects are named — attribute figures to the Bulletin, not to Responsible Statecraft, whose editorial line is restraint-advocacy, and keep its framing out of the piece.

stories.label: Wi-Fi 8 is the first wireless upgrade in years that isn't chasing speed
stories.summary: Wi-Fi 8 (802.11bn) keeps the same peak throughput as Wi-Fi 7 and spends its entire engineering budget on reliability instead — the standard's own name for its goal is Ultra High Reliability, and the target is worst-case latency and packet loss at the edge of coverage, not the headline number on the box. Lead with the reversal, because thirty years of this standard sold megabits: the committee concluded the bottleneck is no longer bandwidth but contention, so the new machinery is coordinated scheduling between neighbouring access points and seamless roaming that stops the handoff drop. Who is affected most, and the reason this matters beyond a router review: the places where Wi-Fi actually carries the internet rather than supplementing fibre — apartment blocks in Karachi, Lagos, Cairo and Jakarta where dozens of radios share the same channel and the failure mode has always been congestion, not link rate. The reader is a developer or network operator: give them what changes concretely, and say plainly that Wi-Fi 8 is a draft standard with certification and silicon still ahead, so nothing shipping today implements it. Aggregated to Hacker News (315 points); the underlying write-up is XDA Developers — cite the standard itself where the claims are technical.

stories.label: Embryonic loss of hexokinase 2 promotes cortical progenitor proliferation and causes autism-like behaviors in mice
stories.summary: Deleting hexokinase 2 — the enzyme that commits glucose to the first step of glycolysis — from the embryonic mouse brain made cortical progenitor cells divide more, and the resulting mice showed autism-like social and repetitive behaviours. Lead with what is surprising to a reader who thinks of neurodevelopment as a genetic program: the variable here is metabolic, not a synapse gene or a transcription factor, and the finding is that how a progenitor cell burns sugar sets how many neurons it makes. The mechanism to explain is the switch between glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation as a proliferation signal — dividing progenitors run on glycolysis, differentiating neurons switch to mitochondrial respiration, so removing the glycolytic commitment step holds cells in the dividing state longer and the cortex ends up wrongly sized. Who this matters to: the reader should get the honest boundary — this is a mouse knockout producing behaviours scored as autism-like on rodent assays, which is a model of a mechanism and not a cause of human autism, and the piece must not let the headline word do work the data cannot. What's next: whether the same metabolic window is sensitive to maternal glucose, which is where the finding would connect to something modifiable. Early-access accepted version; note the DOI is permanent but the text may still change.

stories.label: Rainwater harvest initiative launched in Bajaur, Mohmand
stories.summary: Rooftop rainwater harvesting systems have been installed in Bajaur and Mohmand, two of the tribal districts merged into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2018, starting with government buildings in Civil Colony Khar. Lead with the water arithmetic, not the ribbon-cutting: these districts get most of their annual rainfall in a few monsoon weeks and then run dry, and the constraint is not rainfall volume but storage — a roof of a few hundred square metres captures tens of thousands of litres from a single season that currently runs off into ephemeral streams and is gone. Who is affected: households, overwhelmingly the women and girls who carry water, in districts where the alternative is a deepening tube well in an aquifer that monsoon runoff no longer recharges because it never stops long enough to infiltrate. Who holds power: the additional deputy commissioner's office, which is where the merged districts' development budget is actually spent, and which is why the first installation is on an administrative building rather than a village. The structural why: this is adaptation at the cheapest possible unit cost — a tank, a gutter and a filter against a glacier-and-monsoon water system that is becoming less predictable each decade. Be honest about scale: this is a pilot on public buildings, and the piece should say what it would take to reach households. Single Pakistani source, which is the right regional outlet for the story.

stories.label: Shares flat in Asia before Iran sanctions news, Nvidia results
stories.summary: Consolidated entry: Washington is due to publish the detail of new Iran sanctions today, and Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei answered in advance — if the economic war continues, 'not even one drop of oil' leaves the Strait of Hormuz or the Persian Gulf. Lead with the asymmetry the market is pricing: oil eased and Asian equities sat flat while the party threatening to close a strait carrying roughly a fifth of world seaborne crude was ignored. Who is affected: importers across Asia (Indonesia, India, China) who buy that barrel, not the US Treasury writing the sanction. The mechanism to explain is that a sanctions regime aimed at Iranian export revenue hands Iran a chokepoint threat as its only symmetric reply — the same escalation ladder that produced yesterday's Hormuz transit-charge bill in the Majlis. Follow-up to that story: the fee was the graduated move, this is the maximal one. Do not treat Rezaei's statement as policy — it is a threat by a named official, and should be attributed as such.

stories.label: Shein's Purchase of Everlane Faces US National Security Review
stories.summary: Shein prices a Hong Kong listing of nearly 280 million shares at HK$47.60–49.50 to raise up to HK$13.86bn ($1.77bn) on 1 September — while its purchase of the US brand Everlane goes into a national security review in Washington. Lead with the pairing: the same company is being welcomed as capital in Hong Kong and screened as a security risk in the United States on the same day. Who holds power: CFIUS, which now treats a clothing retailer's US customer data and supply chain as a security object, and the Hong Kong exchange, which has become the listing venue of last resort for Chinese firms shut out of New York. The structural why: fast fashion's value is data and logistics, not garments, which is what makes an apparel deal reviewable at all. Note the cost side that neither the IPO nor the review addresses — the Xinjiang cotton and piece-rate labour questions that have followed Shein since 2021.

stories.label: Piyush Goyal lands in Japan as India eyes ₹60,000 crore investment boost in 10 years
stories.summary: India's commerce minister arrives in Tokyo with a nearly 200-member business delegation against Japan's standing target of ¥10 trillion (about ₹60,000 crore) of investment in India over a decade. Lead with the delegation size, not the ministerial handshake: 200 firms is an attempt to convert a state-to-state number into actual factories, and the ten-year target set last year has so far produced far less. The mechanism worth explaining is semiconductors — Japan holds the materials and equipment tier of the chip supply chain (photoresists, wafers, lithography components) that India's fabs cannot buy from anywhere else at scale, which is why Tokyo, Nagoya and Osaka are on the itinerary rather than only Tokyo. Who is affected: an Indian chip programme whose bottleneck is inputs and skilled process engineers, not capital.

stories.label: Saudi Arabia strikes northern Yemen villages
stories.summary: Saudi artillery shelled villages in the Razih district of Saada province in northern Yemen on Monday, per al-Masirah via Mehr. Continuation of injustice is the development: Saada has been under cross-border bombardment on and off for eleven years, and Razih sits on the border strip where the shelling never fully stopped even during the truce years. Who is affected: farming villages with no air defence and no evacuation route; who holds power: the Saudi-led coalition and the states that sell it the artillery. Write the sourcing honestly — the only account in today's feed is Iranian state media relaying a Houthi-aligned broadcaster, and casualty figures should be reported as claimed, not confirmed. That absence is itself the story's second layer: a Saudi bombardment of Yemeni villages draws no Western wire coverage at all.

stories.label: UK's Burnham to visit Ukraine with plan to support long-range missile production
stories.summary: Britain will allow the European manufacturer MBDA to support long-range missile production with Ukraine, announced as Burnham co-chairs the Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv alongside Zelenskiy. Lead with what changes: this moves Ukraine from a recipient of finished Western missiles to a co-producer, which removes the per-transfer political veto that has governed every deep-strike decision since 2022. Who holds power: MBDA's shareholder governments — the UK, France and Italy — who can now supply a production line instead of a stockpile, and who thereby also lose the ability to throttle usage case by case. The structural why for the reader: weapons transfers are reversible, industrial capacity is not, and a missile plant inside a war zone is also a target.

stories.label: After PM CARES Fund, CJP flags ₹92 crore upkeep bill for ministers' homes: 'Stop fixing lavish homes'
stories.summary: A ₹92 crore public bill for maintaining ministers' Lutyens' Delhi bungalows, set against a campaign demanding electricity, drinking water, toilets and mid-day meals in rural government schools.
